sections.overview: The veined octopus is a small, bottom-living octopus of tropical coastal waters. Its famous use of coconut shells is one of the clearest documented examples of tool carrying by a marine invertebrate.
sections.identification: The oval mantle is brown to orange and marked with pale, dark-edged reticulations that resemble veins; large suckers near the arm bases may look bluish. Published maxima vary: one species account gives 80 mm mantle length and 400 g, while a survey cites 90 mm; these are maxima, not typical adult measurements.
sections.habitat: It shelters in holes in soft sand or mud in very shallow water near the coast.
sections.diet: Stomach observations indicate prawns and fish, although many examined guts were empty or held only traces.
sections.behavior: When travelling over exposed sand, it can walk on two arms with a rolling gait while the other six curl around the body, disguising its outline as a floating coconut or debris. It also carries paired coconut-shell halves and assembles them as a shelter when threatened.
sections.reproduction: Field observations document mating, but do not establish a reliable species-wide breeding season or clutch-size range.
sections.ecology: This benthic predator carries shells that become useful only when assembled as a shelter, so it pays a locomotion cost while transporting them.
sections.conservation: The cited sources describe local fishery catches and field observations but do not provide a global population trend or threat assessment across the Indo-Pacific range.
